title: Comparison for a marked simplicial cylinder
statement:
Use small simplicial categories, the Bergner model homotopy category $h\mathrm{sCat}$, and derived-pushout localization $q:C\to L_WC$ as in [lem-coef-simplicial-inversion-universal-property]. Here $W$ is any set of vertex arrows; $\pi_0$ has the same objects and path components of mapping simplicial sets as morphisms. All displayed categories fit in a fixed sufficiently large universe. Let $A$ be a small simplicial category, $V$ a set of its vertex arrows, and $q:A\to L_VA$ its localization unit. Assume explicitly that $\pi_0q$ is essentially surjective. The cartesian product of simplicial categories is the product described in [lem-coef-simplicial-inversion-product-parameter]. Let $[1]$ be the discrete walking arrow $t:0\to1$ and $\mathbb J$ the discrete groupoid with two objects and exactly one arrow between each ordered pair. In $A\times[1]$ mark the set
$$U=\{(v,1_0),(v,1_1):v\in V\}\ \cup\ \{(1_a,t):a\in\operatorname{Ob}A\}.$$The functor $q\times([1]\to\mathbb J)$ induces an isomorphism
$$\Phi:L_U(A\times[1])\xrightarrow{\sim}(L_VA)\times\mathbb J$$
in $h\mathrm{sCat}$. For $e=0,1$, let $k_e:L_VA\to L_U(A\times[1])$ be induced by the endpoint inclusion. Then $\Phi k_e=\iota_e$ in $h\mathrm{sCat}$, where $\iota_e$ is the corresponding endpoint inclusion into $(L_VA)\times\mathbb J$. This holds without any local Kan, cofibrancy or saturation assumption.

source.place: HTT Lemma A.3.6.17, printed p.904, final interval-inclusion argument, using Lemma A.3.5.14, printed p.896, and Proposition A.3.5.5; below proof paragraph 2 of prop-coef-integral-exceptional-adjoint; online source read; archival copy WANTED. No Stacks tag.

proof.text: First identify the interval localization under $[1]$. Put $i:[1]\to\mathbb J$. For each small target $T$, the walking-groupoid statement identifies restriction $\operatorname{Map}^h(\mathbb J,T)\to\operatorname{Map}^h([1],T)$ with a weak equivalence onto the union of the invertible-arrow components. Taking path components and using the natural bijection with morphisms in $h\mathrm{sCat}$ from the framed-mapping statement, $i^*$ is injective with image precisely the classes inverting $t$. The characterization clause of the inversion universal property therefore identifies $L_{\{t\}}[1]$ with $\mathbb J$ under $[1]$. In particular the identification carries the localization unit to $i$.

source.place: Notation A.3.5.1, Lemma A.3.5.3 and Proposition A.3.5.5, printed pp.891-893; taking components of the cited walking-groupoid function-complex comparison.

proof.text: Write $B=A\times[1]$, $H=\{(1_a,t):a\in\operatorname{Ob}A\}$, $R=\{(v,1_e):v\in V,\ e=0,1\}$, and $s=1_A\times i:B\to A\times\mathbb J$. Apply product-parameter with $C=[1]$, $D=A$, $W=\{t\}$ and interchange the two factors. Its specified marked set is exactly $H$. Cartesian product with $A$ preserves Dwyer--Kan equivalences: by [lem-coef-realization-finite-limits] realization of a product of mapping simplicial sets is the k-space product, whose path components and homotopy groups are products, so a weak homotopy equivalence stays one after product with $A(a,a')$; and $\pi_0(C\times A)=\pi_0C\times\pi_0A$, where the product of an equivalence with an identity is an equivalence. Hence $-\times A$ descends to $h\mathrm{sCat}$ and carries the isomorphism of Step 1 under $[1]$ to an isomorphism $L_{\{t\}}[1]\times A\cong\mathbb J\times A$ under $[1]\times A$; the same functoriality makes the products $q\times i$, $q\times1_{\mathbb J}$ used below classes in $h\mathrm{sCat}$. Together with Step 1, its comparison identifies $L_HB$ with $A\times\mathbb J$ under $B$, with structure map $s$. Consequently, for every $T$, restriction $s^*$ is injective and its image is exactly the homotopy classes $B\to T$ inverting $H$, by the inversion universal property. Both endpoint inclusions are carried to the corresponding endpoint inclusions because these comparisons are under $B$.

source.place: Lemma A.3.5.14, printed p.896, and Proposition A.3.5.5, printed p.893; first product comparison.

proof.text: Put $R_J=\{(v,1_j):v\in V,\ j\in\operatorname{Ob}\mathbb J\}$ and $r=q\times1_{\mathbb J}:A\times\mathbb J\to (L_VA)\times\mathbb J$. Apply product-parameter with $C=A$, $D=\mathbb J$, $W=V$. It identifies $L_{R_J}(A\times\mathbb J)$ with $(L_VA)\times\mathbb J$ under $A\times\mathbb J$. The inversion universal property now says that $r^*$ is injective on morphisms to every $T$, with image exactly those classes inverting $R_J$. Notice that $s$ takes $R$ onto $R_J$: $[1]$ and $\mathbb J$ have exactly the same two objects, and $s(v,1_e)=(v,1_e)$.

source.place: Lemma A.3.5.14, printed p.896, and Proposition A.3.5.5; second product comparison.

proof.text: For a target $T$ and a class $f:B\to T$, Step 2 gives a unique class $g:A\times\mathbb J\to T$ with $gs=f$ if and only if $f$ inverts $H$. For this $g$, the equality $\pi_0g\,\pi_0s\cong\pi_0f$ and the explicit formula $s(v,1_e)=(v,1_e)$ show that $g$ inverts $R_J$ if and only if $f$ inverts $R$. Thus Step 3 extends $g$ uniquely across $r$ precisely when $f$ inverts both $H$ and $R$. Composition of these two injective restriction maps is therefore injective, with image exactly the $U=H\cup R$ inverting classes. By the characterization in the inversion universal property, $( (L_VA)\times\mathbb J,rs)$ is isomorphic under $B$ to $(L_UB,u)$, where $u:B\to L_UB$ is the localization unit. Explicitly the property supplies maps each way under $B$; the two composites restrict to the respective identity maps on $B$, so injectivity makes both composites identities. This gives $\Phi$ with $\Phi u=rs=q\times i$, and proves that it is the induced comparison claimed in the statement.

source.place: Proposition A.3.5.5, printed p.893; explicit composition of the two mapping properties, applied to the interval-inclusion argument of Lemma A.3.6.17, printed p.904.

proof.text: Let $j_e:A\to B$ denote the endpoint inclusion. The functoriality clause of the inversion universal property induces $k_e$ with $k_eq=uj_e$, since $j_e$ takes $V$ into $U$. Hence $(\Phi k_e)q=\Phi uj_e=(q\times i)j_e=\iota_eq$. Restriction along $q$ is injective for the target $(L_VA)\times\mathbb J$, so $\Phi k_e=\iota_e$, for $e=0,1$. All targets and products used above are small in the stipulated universe. The product comparison explicitly allows arbitrary mapping simplicial sets and unsaturated markings; the walking-groupoid statement uses a replacement of the target, imposing no fibrancy assumption on $A$. The extra essential-surjectivity hypothesis on $\pi_0q$ is retained, although this argument does not need it.

The statement is unchanged and introduces its own objects. The essential-surjectivity hypothesis is extra but harmless, and it holds by lem-coef-simplicial-localization-essential-image. Small cases checked: A empty; A a point with V empty (gives 𝕁); V empty; A=[1] with V its arrow (gives 𝕁×𝕁); markings with identities or repeated arrows. Step-by-step results. Step 1: taking π0 of the walking-groupoid weak equivalence onto the union of invertible-arrow components gives the mapping property of (𝕁,i), and the characterization clause then gives 𝕁 ≅ L_{t}[1]. Step 2 had a C3 gap: it multiplied the Step 1 isomorphism in hsCat by A, which needs products to preserve Dwyer–Kan equivalences. That fact appears only in the proof of product-parameter, not in its statement. I fixed it in fixes/dag/nodes/sec-six-functors/lem-coef-simplicial-marked-cylinder-comparison.json by adding the two-line argument and citing lem-coef-realization-finite-limits (same unit, no cycle), and recomputed proof_deps. Step 3: the marked set is exactly R_J, and s(R)=R_J because s(v,1_e)=(v,1_e). Step 4: both directions of the image criterion hold, rs=q×i inverts H and R, and injectivity yields Φ under B. Step 5: k_e q=u j_e, then (q×i)j_e=ι_e q, and injectivity of q^* gives Φk_e=ι_e. Route and duplicates: all citations are in the unit sk-prop-sf-biduality-general, so there are no tool_uses.
